quiz.q: What is the difference between `String` and `&str`?
options: String owns growable text; &str is a borrowed view of existing text
&str owns text; String only borrows it
String is for numbers; &str is for letters
quiz.explain: String owns a growable heap buffer. &str is a borrowed view into text that lives somewhere else.

quiz.q: What type is a string literal like `"hello"`?
quiz.explain: String literals are &str — borrowed views pointing into your compiled program.

quiz.q: For a function that only reads text, which parameter type is most flexible?
options: String, because it owns the data
&str, because both String (via &) and literals can be passed
quiz.explain: Taking &str lets callers pass a borrowed String or a literal without giving up ownership. Take &str to read, return String to build new text.

quiz.q: What does `.len()` return for the string `"café"`?
options: 5, the number of bytes (é takes 2 bytes in UTF-8)
quiz.explain: .len() counts bytes, not characters. 'é' is 2 bytes in UTF-8, so "café" is 5 bytes. Use .chars().count() for the character count.

flashcards.back: String owns growable, heap-allocated text. &str is a borrowed view of text that already exists. String literals are &str.

flashcards.front: Which text type should a read-only function parameter use?
flashcards.back: &str. It accepts both a String (borrowed with &) and a literal, without taking ownership.

flashcards.front: Why can't you write `some_string[0]` to get a character?
flashcards.back: Rust text is UTF-8; byte positions and character positions can differ, so indexing by number is disallowed. Use .chars().nth(i).
No — it gives the byte count. Use .chars().count() for the number of characters.
